item.title: Super Bowl champion, Eagles legend Lane Johnson abruptly retires at 36
item.description: Philadelphia Eagles legend Lane Johnson stunningly announced his retirement from football at the age of 36 in a statement to social media on Tuesday.
item.content:encoded:
Philadelphia Eagles legend and two-time Super Bowl champion Lane Johnson stunningly announced his retirement from the NFL on Tuesday.

Johnson, 36, was a surprise inactive in the Eagles’ 24-20 loss to the Los Angeles Rams on Sunday, and it came out that he was out for unexpected personal reasons. Johnson announced in a statement that he is focusing on his mental health.

"Philadelphia. You truly are the City of Brotherly Love. The best fans and the most prideful city in the entire world. I have given it my all for 14 years; season after season pushing my body to the max and tirelessly working my craft to not only live up to the legacy of the guys that came before me, but to set a new standard of success for the best franchise in all of sports," Johnson said in a statement.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

"I deeply wanted to gut it out for one more year; to take the field with my brothers for one last season. But after a lot of reflection, I’ve realized that my personal and family priorities in my life have changed. Right now, it is critical that I focus on my mental health. I owe it to my teammates, coaches, the organization and the fans to have my head and heart 100 percent in the game. And right now my heart is telling me that it’s time to say goodbye to football."

Johnson was a member of the Eagles’ two Super Bowl-winning teams in 2017 and 2024 and called those rides up Broad Street the ultimate privilege. He thanked the entire Eagles organization for taking a chance on him and the coaches and teammates he played alongside during his 14-year career.

"Right now, what’s most important to me is continuing to focus on my mental health and spending more time with my kids and family," Johnson said.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"But Philadelphia will always be home, and I will forever be an Eagle. Thank you for the love and the enduring support."

The love is reciprocal as owner Jeffery Lurie called him an "all-time Eagle."

"Lane Johnson is an all-time Eagle and one of the best players ever to play his position in NFL history. Lane was a major contributor to our team success for 14 seasons, helping to bring two Super Bowl championships and many other memorable moments to the organization and the city of Philadelphia," Lurie said in a statement.

"Beyond his on-field accomplishments, Lane has done a tremendous amount to give back to the community through his numerous charitable endeavors. The courage he has shown using his own personal experiences to advocate for mental health awareness has undoubtedly saved lives. We appreciate everything Lane has contributed to our organization, and we wish him and his family nothing but the best."

The Eagles will sorely miss Johnson, as they were 98-42-1 in games he played during his career and just 15-29 when he was out of the lineup. In his 14 seasons, he made the Pro Bowl six times.

Johnson was limited to 10 games last season because of an injury, but he had played in all three games prior to missing the Rams game. The Eagles selected Johnson with the No. 4 overall pick in the 2013 NFL Draft out of Oklahoma, and the Texas native emerged as one of the best right tackles in the sport during his career.

item.title: NFL refs have set all-time record for flags this season, and it's changing the outcome of games
item.description: NFL officials have thrown more accepted penalties through Week 4 than any season since 1978, with 17 nullified touchdowns compared to five last year.
item.content:encoded:
Each year, NFL fans complain that officials are throwing more flags than ever before. Most years, the perception exceeds the evidence. This year, the evidence supports the complaint.

The NFL is on a historically high penalty pace.

According to ESPN Insights, the league has recorded more accepted penalties through Week 4 this season than in any other season since play-by-play data became available in 1978.

Week 4 was especially severe. Officials assessed 271 accepted penalties, the second-highest total for any week over that span. That's around 17 accepted penalties per game.

BOMANI JONES CALLS JOSH ALLEN A 'MORON' FOR COSTLY INTERCEPTION, WHILE DEFENDING LAMAR JACKSON FOR SAME THING

Sharp Football Analysis provided additional context on Tuesday. According to its analysis, officials are flagging offenses at the highest per-snap rate through four weeks of any season since 2000, at 6.18 penalties per 100 snaps.

The increase is also occurring at particularly consequential points in games. Officials have set early-season records for accepted flags thrown in the red zone and on third and fourth downs in the second half.

These penalties aren't merely disrupting drives. They are erasing points.

So far this season, penalties have nullified 17 touchdowns. At the same point last year, that number was five. In 2024, it was four.

To be clear, an accepted penalty does not mean officials made the correct call.

Last week, Rams coach Sean McVay said the NFL privately acknowledged that officials incorrectly called defensive pass interference against Los Angeles in the closing moments of its Week 3 loss to Denver, nullifying an interception. Without the flag, the interception would've won the Rams the game. Instead, Denver retained possession and capitalized on the erroneous call to win.

That example illustrates the larger problem.

The proliferation of flags has become one of the defining features of the 2026 season. Fans don't watch football to see officials determine the outcome of drives. Yet listen to almost any broadcast after a significant play, and you'll hear an announcer quickly add, "No flags."

There's a reason for that.

MICHELE TAFOYA DEFENDS HOLLY ROWE AMID ARCH MANNING, STEVE SARKISIAN INCIDENT

Viewers have become conditioned not to trust the initial result of a play. A touchdown, long completion, turnover, or critical stop now routinely produces a moment of hesitation as everyone scans the field for yellow.

Waiting to find out whether a play counts has become part of the viewing experience. It shouldn't be. It's a problem.

Which raises a more important question: Why are officials throwing flags at such a historic rate?

One possibility is that teams are simply playing sloppier football. Reduced offseason work and lighter practice schedules could plausibly contribute to more procedural errors, poor technique, and legitimate penalties.

But football has always operated under an inconvenient reality: officials could probably identify some technical violation on nearly every play.

Some infractions are obvious and materially affect the play. Others occupy a gray area where enforcement depends largely on judgment and discretion.

The distinction matters because officials plainly exercise that discretion later in the season.

The same officiating crews that produce flag-heavy games during the regular season generally adopt a more permissive standard in the playoffs. Officials are more inclined to "let them play" in the postseason, particularly in high-leverage situations where a marginal call could dictate the outcome.

By effectively raising the threshold in the playoffs, the NFL acknowledges that over-officiating diminishes the product and that marginal penalties should not decide its most important games.

That also suggests the league accepts, or at least tolerates, the flag-heavy officiating that has come to define the early months of the season. If it didn't, it would instruct officials to exercise the same restraint in September and October that they routinely exercise in January.

Perhaps the league sees officiating controversy as a marketing tool. Questionable calls generate scrutiny, debate, television segments, social-media engagement, and another news cycle surrounding the NFL.

Or perhaps the increase reflects an institutional tendency toward over-enforcement. Officiating gives referees considerable authority over the game. It stokes their egos.

Whatever the explanation, the league should intervene and stop this immediately.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Obvious infractions should be called. Marginal violations that require slow-motion examination or have no meaningful effect on the play should face a much higher threshold.

What's happening this season is bad for fans, broadcasters, teams and the quality of the sport itself. There are too many flags, too many erased touchdowns, and too many pivotal possessions altered by officiating.

That's particularly difficult to defend at a time when the NFL has never been more expensive or complicated to watch. Between expanded national windows, streaming exclusives, multiple subscriptions, and an increasingly fragmented broadcast schedule, the league is already asking more of consumers than ever before.

In return, the league should at least provide a better product than what it has delivered over four weeks.

Enough with the ticky-tack flags.

item.title: Loyalty be damned: Did these coaches stick around a season too long and blow their chances at a big gig?
item.description: Kenny Dillingham, Jedd Fisch, and Brent Key were among college football's hottest coaching names. Now all three programs are struggling in 2025.
item.content:encoded:
I want to take you all back to January 2025.

The Arizona State Sun Devils just completed an improbable run to the College Football Playoff only two years removed from the disastrous Herm Edwards era.

Head coach Kenny Dillingham, in only his second year on the job, had guided the program through NCAA sanctions and three-win seasons to a Big 12 championship and had his team on the precipice of a Playoff win over Texas thanks to the contributions of exciting players like Cam Skattebo, Jordyn Tyson, and Sam Leavitt.

SLEEPER TEAMS FROM EACH POWER 4 CONFERENCE: WHO WILL EXCEED EXPECTATIONS THIS COLLEGE FOOTBALL SEASON?

Just two years later and the Sun Devils now sit at 2-2 with an anemic offense, fresh off a beatdown at the hands of Baylor, a team currently employing a coach who was on a ridiculously hot seat himself just a month earlier.

Less than a year after Arizona State's magical CFP appearance, two more coaches were making names for themselves at schools on opposite ends of the country.

Jedd Fisch inherited a Washington program in 2024 that had just competed for a national championship the season prior to his arrival, but had to replace almost 100% of the team's production from a year earlier.

After a 6-7 campaign that year showed promise, Fisch followed that up with a nine-win season that included a bowl win over Boise State and featured a quarterback by the name of Demond Williams who was the toast of college football.

LINCOLN RILEY HOT SEAT RUMORS GET LOUDER AFTER 'FIRE LINCOLN' CHANTS DURING USC-WASHINGTON

Meanwhile, more than 2,600 miles to the southeast, Brent Key was turning Georgia Tech into a legitimate threat in the ACC with a super innovative offense and a Heisman hopeful by the name of Haynes King at quarterback.

The Yellow Jackets climbed to as high as number seven in the AP Poll, their highest mark in nearly two decades, and even finished the season ranked for the first time since 2014.

Ten months later, and both Washington and Georgia Tech - along with the aforementioned Sun Devils - look like shells of their former selves from just a season ago.

It happens. These schools are not built to contend for more than a season or two in a row without sharp fluctuations year-to-year.

THERE'S A DIFFERENCE BETWEEN COACHES WHO 'CAN'T' WIN A NATIONAL CHAMPIONSHIP AND COACHES WHO 'HAVEN'T'

While programs like Ohio State, Texas, Oregon, and Georgia have the infrastructure, funding, and talent pipelines to be consistently great year in and year out, the Washingtons, Georgia Techs, and Arizona States of the world need to capitalize on razor thin windows and go "all in" whenever they recognize those windows are approaching.

That goes for their coaches, too.

There was a time when Dillingham, Fisch, and Key were being linked to every major job in college football following their respective "window years."

Dillingham was talked about as Mike Norvell's potential replacement at Florida State following their abysmal 2024 season, and the 36-year-old head coach was even discussed for the Michigan job shortly after they fired Sherrone Moore.

WHICH HEAD COACH'S SEAT IS HOTTER HEADING INTO 2026 SEASON: SHANE BEAMER OR MIKE NORVELL?

Speaking of the Maize and Blue, Fisch was also thought to be the leader in the clubhouse to take the job in Ann Arbor, and both he and Key were heavily considered as candidates for the opening at Florida, with Fisch getting extra attention given his alumni status in Gainesville.

These three coaches were some of the hottest names in the last two hiring cycles, and for whatever reason, they chose to stay at their respective spots.

There's no shame in that, and for Dillingham and Key, it could also come down to the fact that they are coaching at their alma maters.

But the question remains: did they miss their chance to parlay their successful seasons into jobs at bigger, more established programs?

If Washington, Arizona State, and Georgia Tech all finish with six or seven losses each this season, their respective coaches likely won't be fielding many calls when high-level jobs come open in November.

Perhaps they're happy where they are now, although Dillingham has specifically called out Arizona State's fanbase and booster clubs about a lack of funding in the past, and based on conversations I've had with people close to the Gators' football program regarding the Florida job, it's one that Fisch would readily take under the right circumstances.

Time will tell for all three of these coaches, as well as others who are making a name for themselves at the "mid-tier" Power 4 programs.

COLLEGE FOOTBALL WEEK 4 CONTENDERS, PRETENDERS: TEXAS SURVIVES, MICHIGAN'S KARMA AND COACHES ARE SWEATING

Maybe one of these three will win 10 or 11 games in 2027 and land a tier-one job to make me look like a fool.

It worked for Matt Campbell, who had multiple historic seasons at Iowa State in 2020 and 2024 only to turn down other offers.

It was only after Penn State came calling a year later that Campbell finally decided to leave the comfort of Ames.

Patience is a virtue, as is loyalty, but when it comes to being a college football coach, sometimes those things can come back to bite you in the rear end.

You're only as good as your latest season, and a lot of these hiring athletic directors have a bad case of recency bias when it comes to selecting their next football coach.

I'll be interested to see where Kenny Dillingham, Brent Key, and Jedd Fisch are a year from today.

Will they be settling in at cushy new jobs in Tallahassee, Los Angeles, and Norman?

Or will they be the latest victims of the "what have you done for me lately" league that is Power 4 college football?

There's only one way to find out.

item.title: Mother, son among six identified after Boston-bound medevac jet vanishes off Nantucket
item.description: The six people aboard the Latitude Air Ambulance medevac jet that vanished over the Atlantic near Nantucket while en route to Boston have been identified.
item.content:encoded:
The six people aboard a Boston-bound medical jet that disappeared over the Atlantic have been identified as a Bermudian mother and son and a four-person Canadian flight and medical crew.

Marilyn Lavonne Bean, 66, was being transported for treatment related to a stroke, with her son, Sergio Wayne Lottimore, accompanying her aboard the medevac flight.

The U.S. Coast Guard identified the four Canadians aboard as Philip Gregory Childerhose, Thomas Henry Farquhar, Sarah Jane Paton and Jolene Beth Weir.

1 MISSING, 4 RUSHED TO HOSPITAL AFTER HELICOPTER CRASHES OFF SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA ISLAND

Childerhose was the captain and Farquhar was the first officer, while Paton served as the flight nurse and Weir as the respiratory therapist, according to Latitude Air Ambulance.

The Gulfstream G100 disappeared early Saturday while traveling from Bermuda to Boston, triggering a major Coast Guard search off Nantucket. The Coast Guard suspended the search Sunday after debris associated with the aircraft was located.

Lottimore was senior vice president and head of specialty reinsurance at Hamilton Re, according to the Bermuda-based company.

"The entire Hamilton team is heartbroken by the loss of a respected leader, colleague and friend," Hamilton Re said in a statement.

4 FLORIDA FAMILY MEMBERS FOUND DEAD AFTER SMALL PLANE GOES DOWN OFF THE BAHAMAS

Lottimore was also a 2002 graduate of Warwick Academy, where he had served as a prefect. The school remembered him as an "outstanding person."

Bermuda Police said a family liaison officer had been assigned to assist the family.

The aircraft was operated by Latitude Air Ambulance, a Canadian medical transport company. Latitude previously confirmed to Fox News Digital that the Gulfstream was operating as a medevac flight and was expected to make the journey from Bermuda to Boston in approximately two hours.

Latitude Air Ambulance President Peter Byl said the company was mourning an "unimaginable loss."

"Our focus now is on supporting their families, supporting our people and assisting the authorities," Byl said. "We will honour our colleagues by remembering the care, professionalism, and commitment they brought to their work every day."

The flight departed Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport late Friday night and was bound for Boston Logan International Airport.

COAST GUARD PLANE WITH DHS SECRETARY MARKWAYNE MULLIN ON BOARD MAKES EMERGENCY LANDING AFTER ENGINE FAILURE

The Transportation Safety Board of Canada said the crew reported electrical difficulties as the aircraft approached the Boston area before the jet descended rapidly and air traffic control lost contact south of Nantucket.

FlightAware data previously reviewed by Fox News Digital showed the aircraft descending from 24,000 feet to 11,000 feet in roughly three minutes around 1 a.m. Saturday.

The Federal Aviation Administration previously told Fox News Digital that it issued a Search and Rescue Alert Notice at approximately 1:20 a.m. ET. Massport later confirmed the aircraft never arrived at Boston Logan.

A civilian vessel located debris associated with the aircraft, according to the Coast Guard.

"During this incredibly difficult time, our heartfelt condolences go out to the families and friends impacted by this tragic incident," Rear Adm. Matthew Lake, commander of the Coast Guard Northeast District, said Monday.

"We are grateful to the crews and partner agencies who quickly responded to this incident, and we will continue to support our Canadian partners as they conduct their investigation," Lake added.

Canada is leading the investigation because the aircraft was registered there, in accordance with international agreements, according to the TSB. The National Transportation Safety Board is assisting as an accredited representative for the United States.

The cause has not yet been determined.

The U.S. Coast Guard and Bermuda Police did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for additional comment Tuesday.

Fox News Digital's James Cirrione contributed to this report.

item.title: US could play role in united Ireland push after Trump's backing, Irish PM says
item.description: Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the United States could potentially help in a future push for a united Ireland after Trump backed it.
item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — Nearly three decades after the Good Friday Agreement transformed Northern Ireland, Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin said the United States could potentially play a role in a future push for a united Ireland following President Donald Trump's backing for reunification.

Martin, whose Fianna Fáil party supports Irish unity, said the landmark 1998 agreement – which largely ended 30 years of sectarian violence in Northern Ireland known as "the Troubles" – created a peaceful mechanism for deciding Northern Ireland's constitutional future, but cautioned that the deep divide between Northern Ireland's nationalist and unionist communities must first be bridged.

"I believe in unity and my party believes in unity, but we have to work on it," Martin told Fox News Digital in an exclusive interview. "We have to build reconciliation amongst the different traditions on the island of Ireland."

"The U.S. were critical to the success of peace and conflict resolution in Ireland," Martin added.

IRISH PM REJECTS ANTISEMITISM CONCERNS IN IRELAND AMID DRAMATIC VOTE OVER BOYCOTTING ISRAEL GAME

Martin spoke to Fox News Digital during the U.N. General Assembly in New York at what he described as a global "crossroad," with war raging in Ukraine, conflict across the Middle East and negotiations underway over Iran and the Strait of Hormuz.

Throughout the interview, he repeatedly returned to Ireland's own experience of conflict and peace as a guide to how the country approaches crises abroad, while defending the country's longstanding policy of military neutrality despite its growing support for Ukraine.

The constitutional question of Irish unity gained renewed attention during Trump's recent visit to Ireland last month, when the president said he would "love" to see Ireland unified and predicted it would eventually happen.

Asked during the Fox News Digital whether Washington could play a role again if Ireland eventually moves toward reunification, Martin replied: "To a degree maybe, potentially, yeah."

Martin spoke before the latest confrontation over Garvaghy Road erupted in Portadown, Northern Ireland, reviving one of Northern Ireland's most bitter marching disputes and underscoring how potent nationalist-unionist divisions remain.

The Parades Commission last month approved a limited Orange Order march along the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road for the first time in 28 years. Residents and supporters blocked the route, while police declined to force the parade through amid fears of serious disorder.

The Orange Order is a Protestant organization whose members generally support Northern Ireland remaining part of the United Kingdom, while many residents of the mainly nationalist Garvaghy Road community, who are predominantly Catholic, favor a united Ireland.

The standoff has since spilled into the courts and Stormont, where parliament meets, as efforts to broker a compromise continue.

Under the Good Friday Agreement, a referendum can be called if it appears a majority in Northern Ireland would support reunification. But Martin said more work is needed to define what a united Ireland would look like and deepen engagement on both sides of the border.

IRISH PM SAYS IRELAND ‘NOT OVERRUN’ BY IMMIGRANTS, LEGAL MIGRATION TIED TO ECONOMIC SUCCESS

UKRAINE AND THE SEARCH FOR PEACE

For Martin, however, the lessons of Northern Ireland's peace process extend far beyond the island.

"Because of our conflict in Northern Ireland, we feel we can make a contribution to that conflict resolution pathway," Martin said.

He said Ireland's experience ending decades of violence now shapes how it approaches Russia's war in Ukraine, the conflict in the Middle East and Europe's increasingly uncertain security environment.

"We don't get a sense that Russia is really interested at this particular stage," Martin said of efforts to end the war in Ukraine.

Martin, who had met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy the previous evening, nevertheless argued that continued channels between Washington and Moscow were important.

Asked whether a realistic peace settlement would ultimately require Ukraine to surrender territory to Russia, Martin rejected the premise.

"Ukraine can't cede territory that Russia hasn't even conquered, despite four years of war," Martin said.

But he said a ceasefire along existing battle lines could provide a starting point for negotiations.

"If we even could get a ceasefire on existing lines, and then negotiations to start," Martin said, adding that Kyiv would need protections against renewed Russian aggression. "Ukraine needs security guarantees."

Martin also pointed to Ukraine's path toward European Union membership as potentially providing an additional layer of security and said the broader security architecture between Europe and Russia would ultimately have to be addressed in negotiations.

"From our perspective, no one has the right to go into another country and take its territory," Martin said.

HOW NEUTRAL IS IRELAND?

Ireland's extensive support for Kyiv, however, raises a more contentious question at home: how far can a militarily neutral country support one side in a war while maintaining that neutrality?

Ireland has committed more than $754 million in humanitarian assistance, military training and other non-lethal support to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022 while stopping short of providing lethal weapons.

Fox News Digital asked Martin whether that level of support undermined Ireland's neutrality.

"No, because we don't give lethal aid, we haven't given military weaponry, but we have given non-lethal assistance in terms of training and so on like that, and also humanitarian aid to Ukraine," Martin said.

Ireland has also taken in large numbers of Ukrainians fleeing the war. Martin said more than 120,000 had arrived at one point, with roughly 80,000 remaining in the country at the time of the interview.

"That's not taking sides, that's taking humanitarian response to a war," Martin said. "And many are contributing, many are working in the economy."

Ireland's neutrality has also faced scrutiny over the long-standing use of Shannon Airport by the U.S. military.

NATO's top military commander, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, described Shannon in August as a "very important logistics hub" for the United States and said withdrawing American military access would probably damage U.S.-Irish relations.

The airport's role has long drawn protests from Irish neutrality campaigners, who argue that allowing U.S. military personnel and aircraft to transit through a civilian airport undermines the country's neutral status.

Despite differing approaches to conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, Martin described the U.S.-Ireland relationship in almost familial terms.

"There's a very strong bond between Ireland and the United States," Martin said.

He pointed to the long-standing tradition of Irish leaders visiting the White House on St. Patrick's Day and the enormous Irish-American diaspora, which he estimated at roughly 30 million people.

"It's just family, there's kinship ties," Martin said.

MIDDLE EAST

Martin said Ireland's peace-process experience also informs its approach to the Middle East, where Dublin has emerged as one of Israel's strongest European critics.

He condemned Hamas' Oct. 7 terrorist attack and defended Israel's right to security while arguing that the subsequent Israeli military campaign in Gaza had been "absolutely disproportionate."

"We believe in a two-state solution," Martin said. "We believe that Israel, of course, has a right to exist in security and its people need to be guaranteed of security. But likewise, Palestinians should have a right to live in their homeland in a peaceful way."

Martin said Ireland's strongly anti-Israel position was shaped partly by its own history and what he described as a "sense of right and justice and fairness."

WATCH: Irish PM explains Ireland's position on Israel, rejects antisemitism concerns amid controversial soccer match

TRUMP'S INVESTMENT PUSH HITS EUROPE AS IRISH PM EYES NEXT TARIFF BREAK

EUROPE'S SECURITY

Ireland currently holds the rotating presidency of the Council of the European Union, placing Martin at the center of negotiations as Europe confronts its biggest security challenges in decades.

"There's a big realization in Europe that we have to do more to provide greater security to Europe, particularly because of the Russian-Ukrainian war," Martin said.

He pointed particularly to Baltic and Nordic countries, where governments have increased defense spending amid fears about Russia.

"Many have an existential fear of Russia," Martin said.

Martin said Europe was also tightening its approach to immigration, echoing comments he made elsewhere in the interview that asylum applications had fallen across Ireland and that governments across the continent were responding to mounting political pressure.

For Martin, those challenges — from Ukraine and the Middle East to Ireland's own unfinished constitutional future —ultimately return to the lessons he believes his country learned through decades of conflict and the peace process that followed.

"The world needs to try and turn a page towards a more peaceful sort of coexistence," Martin said.

item.title: Former Hamas hostage counters Hasan Piker’s UT Austin event with her story of survival
item.description: Former Hamas hostage Maya Regev spoke at UT Austin on the same night Twitch streamer Hasan Piker addressed the University Democrats on campus.
item.content:encoded:
Controversial Twitch streamer Hasan Piker made waves with his visit to the University of Texas at Austin before he even made it into the Lone Star State. 

While he was speaking at an event last week hosted by University Democrats, a student group, another speaker with a much different point of view was telling her story of survival. Former Hamas hostage Maya Regev spoke to students with the goal of ensuring that they hear from someone who witnessed the horrors of Oct. 7, 2023, firsthand.

In a recent conversation with Fox News Digital, Regev took issue with one of Piker's infamous remarks that "It doesn’t matter if rapes f---ing happened on Oct. 7, like that doesn’t change the dynamic for me."

HAMAS USED SEXUAL VIOLENCE 'DELIBERATELY AND SYSTEMATICALLY' ON OCT 7, COMMISSION REPORT FINDS

Regev said students concerned about cases like the sexual assault allegations against Cornell fraternity members may be listening to a person who's said "rape doesn't matter."

Asked about his controversial remarks about the reported rapes committed by Hamas on Oct. 7, Piker told The New Republic that there was "definitely testimony of sexual violence that had taken place amongst the hostages. But that doesn’t change the dynamic of Israel committing a genocide against the Palestinians, and my opposing that genocide."

Regev told Fox News Digital that Chabad, a Jewish organization with representatives across the globe, reached out to her about speaking at UT Austin after Piker's visit to the university was announced.

"I'm not here to silence anyone," Regev told Fox News Digital. "I came there to let people hear what I've been through, like the other side of the story, with facts, with pictures, with records."

UNIVERSITY EVENT WITH HASAN PIKER IN TEXAS DRAWS BACKLASH FROM BOTH SIDES OF THE AISLE

The Anti-Defamation League has criticized Piker for what it calls his "antisemitic conspiracy theories and tropes," and has a list of some of his remarks about Oct. 7, including posting that Hamas hostage and American-Israeli soldier Edan Alexander had volunteered for the "Nazi army."

Regev said that while Piker has freedom of speech and "can say whatever he wants," it was important for her to make sure students were getting more than one point of view. Regev also emphasized the fact that she was speaking from her own experience, not things she read about from others.

"For me, Oct. 7, it's not a debate, it's not something I read online. It's something that I've lived through, something that will forever be inside me, something that I will have to live with for the rest of my life," Regev told Fox News Digital. "I just think that it's important for them to understand that behind every story there are real human beings."

"I was a hostage. I was a Hamas hostage," Regev told Fox News Digital. "I was being held by Hamas, by those monsters, and I think that students might, you know, forget that they are actually real human beings, real families that lost their lives, real women that got raped, men, lives were destroyed on Oct. 7."

Regev pushed back on Piker and other online influencers shaping students' opinions without firsthand knowledge.

"When they hear an influencer post something, when they read something, it's important for them to check the facts before they are repeating a slogan or celebrating death of innocent people," Regev said.

She later added, "I sat with those people. I lived with them for two months, with Hamas people... I think that people should listen to a person who was really there and not to a person who just sees stuff online and has millions of followers."

When asked what influencers like Piker get wrong about the situation in Gaza, she said that they overlook the realities on the ground, particularly Hamas' use of Palestinian civilians as human shields.

"Hamas is using children and women and elderly women as a human shield," Regev said. "I think, again, people should know the facts before they're talking, and especially when you're very influencing."

HASAN PIKER'S DEFENSE OF HAMAS HAVING 'RIGHT TO RESIST MILITARILY' DRAWS CONDEMNATION FROM HUMAN RIGHTS GROUPS

On Oct. 7, 2023, Regev went to the Nova Music Festival with her brother Itay Regev and her friend Omer Shem Tov. When the rocket alerts began sounding at 6:29 a.m., Regev was not so alarmed, explaining, as someone who grew up in Israel, it was something she had experienced several times before that day.

"We thought it was just a matter of time before everything will calm down, and we can keep on partying, but after some time we understood that it [was] a lot more serious than what we thought," she said.

Regev explained that the group headed toward their cars before being told by police officers to abandon their vehicles and that terrorists had invaded the country. That's when Regev, her brother and Shem Tov began running for what she estimated to be 60 to 90 minutes. They then got a call from Ori Danino, a friend of a friend who was also at the festival. Danino had already gotten out of the danger zone, but decided to turn around and pick up the group to get them to safety. Unfortunately, all of them would be abducted and taken to Gaza.

The group drove for about five minutes before "a big pickup truck" with terrorists began shooting at them, hitting Regev in both of her legs. Her brother was also shot. The terrorists dragged Regev, her brother and Shem Tov out of the vehicle before loading them into the pickup truck and driving them into Gaza. While Danino was initially able to escape, he was later caught by another group of terrorists and taken into the Strip.

The Regev siblings were released from captivity in late November 2023, within a few days of each other.

Regev described her release from Gaza as bittersweet, feeling grateful to be home while worrying about her friends who were left behind.

"It was a total shock. I thought that Omer will return home, like, a few days after me, but then the ceasefire was stopped. So, it was very hard for me. I couldn't believe that I escaped this hell, and they are still there being held, Ori, Omer, all the other hostages," Regev told Fox News Digital.

HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA

"I felt very guilty that I was saved, that I'm back home with my family. I can get the medical treatment that I needed to receive and there are people there suffering, still hostages suffering, not eating, being abused physically and mentally. But I understood that I have a voice now, and I have to use it, and I'll do anything in my [power] to bring them back home," she added.

Danino would survive 11 months in captivity before terrorists executed him, along with Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Eden Yerushalmi, Carmel Gat, Almog Sarusi and Alexander Lobanov. Shem Tov endured 505 days in Hamas captivity and was released on Feb. 22, 2025.

With her brother and Shem Tov back home, Regev is finally able to look to the future, something she wasn't mentally ready to do until all the hostages were returned. Now, she's enjoying the simple things in life, walking outside, looking up at the sky.

"I just want to do everything that makes me happy," Regev told Fox News Digital. "When I was there in captivity, I promised myself that I will live life. I told myself that if I'll ever be home again, I'll live life, and I'll study, and I'll go travel the world, and I'd be with friends and my family. And it's what I'm doing now, you know, I'm just doing whatever makes me happy."

"I think that the only thing I wish for myself is to be happy forever and grateful for everything that I have."

item.title: Patriots receiver's girlfriend celebrates his game-winning touchdown by peeing her pants

item.content:encoded:

"An elevated guy made a hell of a catch. Probably won't hear from him again. Respectfully," is part of what Gardner-Johnson had to say.

TRAVIS KELCE REACTS TO TAYLOR SWIFT'S VIRAL 'THAT'S MY HUSBAND' MOMENT DURING WIN OVER COLTS

item.title: Comeback canceled: Seahawks ditch plan to sign veteran RB Joe Mixon after failed physical
item.description: Joe Mixon's NFL comeback stalled after the Seattle Seahawks declined to sign him following a failed physical, turning to Robert Henry Jr. instead.
item.content:encoded:
So much for Joe Mixon’s NFL return.

After bringing the 30-year-old running back in for a workout, the Seattle Seahawks decided not to sign Mixon to their practice squad after his physical, multiple reports said early Tuesday.

Instead, the reigning Super Bowl champions plan to sign Robert Henry Jr. off the Washington Commanders' practice squad.

SEATTLE SEAHAWKS THROW JOE MIXON ANOTHER CHANCE IN THE NFL FOLLOWING BACKFIELD DISASTER

Seattle needs backfield depth despite a 30-23 Week 4 win over the Chargers to reach 3-1.

Rookie Jadarian Price is on IR with a chest injury, and Zach Charbonnet is recovering from a torn ACL (though his 21-day practice window opened Thursday).

Emanuel Wilson shined against L.A. with 120 total yards and two touchdowns, but head coach Mike Macdonald still needs insurance.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Failing his physical is a massive red flag. Mixon missed all of 2025 recovering from a severe foot injury, wiping out momentum from his 1,000-yard, 11-touchdown Pro Bowl season with Houston in 2024.

In seven seasons with Cincinnati, he won the 2018 AFC rushing title (1,168 yards) and earned a Pro Bowl nod in 2021 during their Super Bowl LVI run. He backed that up in 2024 with Houston with his second Pro Bowl selection.

Now, after missing all of 2025 and seeing his Seattle deal fall apart before it started, Mixon's path back to an NFL roster looks tougher than ever.

item.title: Cristiano Ronaldo Is Not Retiring, Blames Coach Jorge Jesus For Portugal Walkout
item.description: Cristiano Ronaldo is not following Lionel Messi into international retirement just yet.
item.content:encoded:
Cristiano Ronaldo is not following Lionel Messi into international retirement just yet.

The Portugal superstar said he will remain available to play for his national team, despite having walked out on the squad during the current international window.

In a long statement issued through the Portuguese media Tuesday, Ronaldo said recently hired coach Jorge Jesus had not been true to his word about when he would play the striker in the latest round of Nations League matches.

Still, the 41-year-old Ronaldo said he owed his teammates an apology and expects to receive a punishment.

"I can promise all my fans, and naturally especially all Portuguese people, that we will have one or more farewell matches. There will be time for that," Ronaldo said.

He added: "Therefore, if I am physically fit, playing for my club, hopefully scoring goals, then after serving whatever suspension is imposed on me, I will be available, as I have always been until today, to compete and win for our national team."

Ronaldo said he had agreed to a plan for managing his playing time and that he expected the coach to publicly clarify the situation and accept responsibility. He said Jesus did not follow through and instead spoke aggressively at a press conference, causing a breakdown of trust.

Reporting by The Associated Press.

item.title: Newsom signs first-in-nation law forcing major companies to reveal slavery-era ties: 'Make it public'
item.description: California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a first-in-the-nation law requiring large companies to disclose slavery-era transactions dating back to 1849.
item.content:encoded:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed a first-in-the-nation law Wednesday requiring large companies doing business in the state to scour historical records and publicly disclose slavery-era transactions, advancing California's broader reparations effort through a new corporate "accountability" mandate.

Newsom’s office referred Fox News Digital to an Oct. 1 interview with civil rights attorney Bryan Stevenson, in which the governor signed the bill on camera and framed the measure as an effort to establish accountability through public disclosure.

"This is a bill that requires large companies that operated before 1965 to search their records for ties to slavery going back to 1849 and then we make it public. These are insurance policies on enslaved people. Human beings used as collateral, quite literally as collateral for loans. Accountability, as Bryan said, starts with the truth," Newsom said.

CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS

Assembly Bill 2599, authored by Democratic Assemblymember Isaac Bryan, applies to businesses with more than $100 million in annual worldwide gross receipts that existed, or have a predecessor company that existed, on or before Dec. 31, 1964. Once funded by the Legislature, covered companies must submit affidavits under penalty of perjury verifying searches for records involving the purchase or sale of enslaved people, their use as loan collateral, slave-related insurance and other transactions.

The law also calls for the records to become publicly accessible through a state digital platform. For companies doing business in California as of Jan. 1, 2028, the first affidavits are due by Jan. 15, 2029, or later if the state's platform has not yet been developed.

Bryan framed the measure as an effort to expose corporate wealth tied to slavery while presenting the bill before lawmakers in June.

"For centuries, private corporations across the country benefited from chattel slavery," Bryan said during a Senate Standing Committee on Public Safety hearing. "They benefited from the economic wealth transfer of free labor."

TRUMP ADMIN WANTS TO STOP ILLINOIS CITY'S REPARATIONS EFFORT FOR 'SIMPLY HANDING OUT MONEY BASED ON RACE'

Fox News Digital reached out to Bryan for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

The law came three years after California's first-in-the-nation Reparations Task Force issued more than 100 recommendations for addressing the effects of slavery and discrimination. The task force examined potential monetary compensation alongside policy changes involving housing, education, policing, health and economic disparities.

Newsom previously stopped short of endorsing the task force’s proposed direct cash payments. In a 2023 statement to Fox News Digital, the governor said addressing slavery’s legacy extended beyond sending checks to eligible residents.

"Dealing with that legacy is about much more than cash payments," Newsom said at the time.

CASH PAYMENTS ARE NOT 'RULED OUT' AS CALIFORNIA COUNTY OFFICIALS PUSH REPARATIONS FOR BLACK LOCALS

The task force's report cited JPMorgan Chase as one historical example, noting the banking giant apologized in 2005 after research found two predecessor banks had accepted approximately 13,000 enslaved people as collateral for loans and eventually took ownership of about 1,250 people when borrowers defaulted.

The legislation faced opposition from several insurance industry groups, including the American Council of Life Insurers and American Property Casualty Insurance Association. California has required insurers to research and disclose slavery-era insurance policies since 2000, and the state maintains those records through its Department of Insurance.

The California Senate Judiciary Committee’s analysis of the bill said five insurance industry groups opposed the bill, including the American Council of Life Insurers, the Association of California Life and Health Insurance Companies and the American Property Casualty Insurance Association. The committee analysis summarized their opposition as focused on potential duplication of slavery-era disclosures insurers were already required to make under a 2000 law.

"AB 2599 appears to require reporting that substantially overlaps with the work already completed pursuant to SB 2199 and codified in CA INS 13810," the opponents said.

item.title: Steak 'n Shake makes major change to burger ingredient as chain continues MAHA push
item.description: Fast-food chain Steak 'n Shake now drenches all buns in pure "Grade AA Wisconsin butter" after ditching seed oils as part of the Make America Healthy Again push.
item.content:encoded:
Steak 'n Shake is now ridding its buns of seed oils.

"Starting today, all Steak 'n Shake buns are officially seed-oil free," the fast-food chain announced Monday in a post on X. "The buns are now unapologetically drenched in pure Grade AA Wisconsin butter."

The bun change is the latest in a series of moves by Steak 'n Shake, which has about 400 locations nationwide, to overhaul its ingredients and align itself with the MAHA movement.

STEAK 'N SHAKE TAPS MAHA OFFICER AS FAST-FOOD CHAIN JOINS RFK JR'S PUSH TO OVERHAUL AMERICAN DIET

In June, Steak 'n Shake made the switch to grass-fed beef and began frying chicken tenders, onion rings and tots in 100% beef tallow.

"In my opinion, real ingredients taste better than the synthetic additives," Michael Boes, the chain's chief MAHA officer, told Fox News.

The chain also has a page on its website dedicated to its transition away from seed oils and its efforts to provide more natural ingredients.

Aside from a "commitment to remove seed oils," the page touts offering cane sugar Coca-Cola and its switch to a2 milk last December.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Reaction to the news was largely positive.

"MAKE AMERICA HEALTHY AGAIN," U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace, R-S.C., commented on X. 

Another X user wrote, "Thank you for listening to the people! Amazing."

"I haven't enjoyed one of your burgers in quite some time," one commenter said. "I look forward to trying this change!"

Seed oils — plant-based cooking oils that are regularly used in processed and packaged foods — are a hot topic in the food and nutrition landscape.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

U.S. Health and Human Services (HSS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been an outspoken critic of seed oils.

Other health agencies have said that seed oils are not so bad. The American Heart Association (AHA) stated in 2024 that "there's no reason to avoid seed oils and plenty of reasons to eat them."

Board-certified family physician Cate Shanahan told Fox News Digital in 2025 that while some seed oils, such as flax oil and sesame seed oil, have nutritional value, there are certain varieties of which people should steer clear.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Shanahan advised that Americans try to stay away from what she calls "the hateful eight seed oils," which include corn, canola, cottonseed, soy, sunflower, safflower, rice bran and grapeseed.

Fox News Digital reached out to Steak 'n Shake for comment.

item.title: Macron trashes American free speech as riots grip France — internet unloads: ‘Enormous fool’
item.description: French President Emmanuel Macron called American free speech "the opposite of free speech" as student protests and school fires sweep across France.
item.content:encoded:
French President Emmanuel Macron is drawing fierce online backlash after criticizing the American conception of free speech and arguing that liberty requires a "common framework" — remarks landing as his government faces mounting pressure from nationwide student protests, school blockades and clashes with riot police across France.

"The so-called American ‘free speech’ today, which some people have promoted, is the opposite of free speech," Macron said at Complutense University in Madrid during a discussion on democracy, youth and the digital age on Sept. 29, according to a translation of his remarks.

Macron argued that free speech is not absolute and must be bounded by the rights of others and respect for public order, while also arguing that the flow of information must maintain a relationship to truth. He compared those limits to restrictions against assaulting or insulting others or destroying public property.

FRANCE’S TEEN RIOTS TAKE EXPLOSIVE NEW TURN AS GOVERNMENT POINTS FINGER AT HARD LEFT

"There is no freedom if there is no limit to my freedom, which begins with the freedom of others and respect for a common framework. I know this when I walk down the street: my freedom cannot mean hitting you, insulting you or trashing the public space we all share," Macron added, according to a translation to English.

The remarks quickly drew backlash online, with critics seizing on the contrast between Macron’s comments on free speech and the unrest unfolding at home, where protests, blockades and clashes with police are testing his government.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

"These people are going to cling to power even if it means burning their countries to the ground," said Federalist senior editor John Daniel Davidson.

"Offended by the First Amendment while completely ignoring the fact his own country is literally burning to the ground," wrote one person.

"His country is being destroyed by riots. Does he consider that free speech," asked another person.

"Emmanuel Macron is an enormous fool," said Wikipedia co-founder Larry Sanger.

"Europeans are so stupid about speech," said one user.

"At this point, bringing back the Bourbons would be more dignified for France," wrote Republican Utah Sen. Mike Lee’s communication director Billy Gribbin.

"The worst president France has ever had, verging on treasonous given his attempts to shut down the nation's remarkable nuclear industry and expertise," wrote Institute of Public Affairs senior fellow Adam Creighton.

"We are still free in America and @EmmanuelMacron can pound sand," wrote Dan Gainor.

FRANCE’S VIOLENT STUDENT PROTESTS RAISE WARNING FOR AMERICA: ‘A CAUTIONARY TALE’

Macron has previously taken aim at the American conception of free speech, declaring that "free speech is pure bulls—" if people do not know how algorithms are guiding what they see online, while calling for greater transparency and "a sort of public order" to curb racist and hate speech during a Feb. 18, appearance in New Delhi, India.

Protests erupted in the Paris suburbs in mid-September over teacher shortages and school resources before rapidly spreading nationwide.

Demonstrators have set fires, damaged buildings and clashed with police while France’s Education Ministry said classes were fully or partially suspended at 891 schools Tuesday, while 24 schools have been burned or ransacked since the protests began, according to the Associated Press.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House for comment.

'Nightcaps' is a daily column that catches you up on the biggest sports, news and culture stories you may have missed while pretending to do work at your desk. It runs Monday-Friday on OutKick.com.

For all of you, it is Tuesday. For me, it's Friday.

You remember Gia Duddy, right? She went ultra mega viral as Will Levis' hot girlfriend during the 2023 NFL Draft — until they broke up five minutes later, Levis publicly professed his love for mayonnaise and then Gia became an influencer. There was also that video leak... but we won't go there.

Anyway, now she's dating Bengals wide receiver Andrei Iosivas.

And I know this because Iosivas confirmed it himself while fighting with some random dude in Gia's Instagram comments.

It started when Gia posted photos from Sunday's Bengals game, and someone commented asking who her mystery man was. Another guy responded, "WR45 on the depth chart Andrei Iosivas."

Which is objectively a pretty funny way to answer that question.

Iosivas, however, did not find it funny.

"plz get ur husband off my girls page," he responded, tagging the guy's wife.

Oh, we're doing this.

The guy fired back that Iosivas should "get back to running special teams coverage" and said Gia had been "passed around half the league."

Gia then jumped in herself, tagged the wife AGAIN and called the guy a great role model for his daughters.

From there, it just got nastier, and I'm not going to reprint the whole thing here. But I do appreciate finding out about a new relationship via an NFL wide receiver fighting for his life in his girlfriend's Instagram comments.

Gia does seem to be settling nicely into her second stint as an NFL WAG, though.

Well, except for one small problem. She has to live in Ohio.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

Apparently eating Skyline Chili and going to King's Island whenever you want aren't selling points for everyone.

In an NFL where players arrive to the stadium decked out in designer outfits and carrying $20,000 Louis Vuitton bags (what are they even carrying in there?), you have to respect Brock Purdy's commitment to showing up every Sunday dressed like a Kohl's ad.

Mr. Irrelevant. Forever humble.

Apparently, Purdy's game-day fits have become enough of a thing that his wife, Jenna, showed him a post from a 49ers fan roasting his fashion choices.

But this man is not trying to make a fashion statement. He just wants to be comfortable, darn it!

And, honestly, Brock Purdy can show up to Levi's Stadium in cargo shorts, Crocs and a Kirkland Signature polo for all I care. The 49ers are 4-0, and through four weeks, he's playing as well as any quarterback in football.

The NFL's own QB rankings have him at No. 1.

Meanwhile, here in Tennessee, the Titans would settle for a quarterback who shows up dressed like the guy changing your oil at Jiffy Lube if he could win a football game.

And at this point, Jiffy Lube guy might actually be an upgrade over Cam Ward.

Not that I have any room to talk as a fan of the God-forsaken Miami Dolphins. Tankathon 2026, baby!

item.title: Ex-CIA officer found with over $40M in gold bars pleads guilty to $194M fraud
item.description: David J. Rush fabricated military credentials to climb CIA ranks, then siphoned $194 million in taxpayer dollars into gold bars and luxury watches.
item.content:encoded:
A former high-ranking CIA official who embezzled nearly $200 million from the federal government lied about his military background and education to climb the ranks at the spy agency, federal prosecutors revealed.

David J. Rush pleaded guilty in Virginia federal court to one count of wire fraud. His plea comes months after an FBI raid on his home uncovered 298 gold bars worth $46 million, $2.1 million in cash and dozens of luxury items.

"Federal employees are entrusted with serving the American people, not themselves," said Attorney General Todd Blanche. "The Trump Administration is committed to rooting out waste, fraud, and abuse in the federal government, including by prosecuting those who foolishly defraud American taxpayers."

UFO WHISTLEBLOWER CLAIMS BILLIONS IN SECRET SPENDING HIDDEN FROM CONGRESS

To reach the upper echelons of the CIA and secure top-secret clearances, Rush fabricated extensive credentials.

On official job applications, he claimed to be a graduate of the U.S. Air Force Test Pilot School and the director of test operations for a joint Army/Navy unit.

In reality, Rush was never a pilot, held no FAA licenses, and served primarily as an information systems technician during his time in the Navy.

Once positioned in senior leadership, Rush executed a massive siphon of taxpayer dollars. He created fictitious government entities and fake initiatives — including a phony "Special Access Program" — to redirect federal funds into his own accounts, ultimately stealing $194 million, according to the Justice Department.

MILLIONS SAVED BY BLOCKING DEAD PEOPLE PAYOUTS AS TRUMP TREASURY DROPS HAMMER ON FEDERAL FRAUD

Rush funneled $145 million into wire transfers to fund an extravagant lifestyle. He purchased high-end real estate, luxury vehicles, and massive quantities of physical gold.

"Rush abused his position and betrayed the public trust and should be held fully accountable for his actions," said CIA Director John Ratcliffe. "Following an internal investigation that identified potential crimes, CIA immediately referred this matter to the FBI."

Under the terms of his plea agreement, Rush agreed to forfeit all assets seized during the investigation. The forfeiture includes the 298 gold bars, $2.1 million in cash, his real estate holdings, 30 luxury watches, predominantly Rolexes, and two 2026 BMW Alpina vehicles — one valued at $172,000.

Rush is scheduled to be sentenced on Jan. 28, 2027. He faces up to 20 years in prison.

Fox News Digital's Alexandra Koch contributed to this report.

item.title: FBI investigated mom over ties to ‘right-wing’ Moms for Liberty group, bombshell DOJ report reveals
item.description: Tina Descovich says Moms for Liberty feels vindication after a DOJ report revealed the FBI opened 25 "Guardian assessments" targeting parents.
item.content:encoded:
Moms for Liberty co-founder Tina Descovich says her organization feels "vindication" after a new Justice Department report revealed the FBI opened dozens of assessments involving parents following a controversial Biden-era directive targeting threats against school officials, including an investigation stemming from a tip that cited one mother's membership in a "right-wing mom’s group."

"My reaction and our reaction at Moms for Liberty is vindication," Descovich told Fox News Digital. "We feel… we're finally being heard."

Descovich said parents involved with her organization became fearful of speaking publicly after the Justice Department and FBI's response to heated school board battles beginning in 2021, claiming some received calls asking about their mental health and whether they had weapons in their homes.

UNEARTHED DOJ EMAILS EXPOSE TURMOIL OVER BIDEN-ERA MEMO URGING CRACKDOWN ON PARENTS

"Parents were afraid to show up," Descovich said. "They were afraid to lose their jobs. They were members of our organization, sometimes privately and silently standing with us, but too afraid to speak out because of what our government did in the United States of America. We need to not forget where we were in 2021 as we go into these midterm elections."

The Justice Department's Weaponization Working Group reported Monday that the FBI opened 25 "Guardian assessments" involving parents following then-Attorney General Merrick Garland's Oct. 4, 2021, memorandum addressing threats against school officials.

BIDEN-ERA FBI TRACKED TRUMP FAMILY TRAVEL AND WILES’ CALLS WITH LAWYERS IN SECRET PROBE: DOCS

The report says an FBI whistleblower disclosed that one mother was investigated following a tip that noted she was a gun owner and belonged to what was described as a "right-wing mom's group." A separate joint DOJ-Education Department release identified that organization as Moms for Liberty.

"We have known since 2021 that the DOJ and the FBI under the Biden administration were basically enemies to parents and to Moms for Liberty," Descovich said. "Our parents were getting phone calls after attending school board meetings asking if they had mental health problems, if they had weapons in their home. They were given case numbers and file numbers. And this latest report that's come out and press release from the DOJ and the DOE acknowledging that fact and declaring that, officially, parents are not domestic terrorists. It's almost ridiculous. It's absurd that that's happened in America and that has to be the headline today that we're actually returning to normalcy."

JUDGE SAYS ISSUES IN TRUMP ADMINISTRATION ANTI-WEAPONIZATION CASE 'ALIVE AND KICKING' DESPITE DOJ PUSH

The press release from the Department of Justice reported that personnel internally called the effort "ridiculous," raised First Amendment concerns and said it appeared political, but that emails show Attorney General Garland issued the memo, persuaded by the Biden White House officials.

The Working Group found that the memo, according to the DOJ press release, "was the product of pressure exerted by the White House and wrongly weaponized the Department of Justice against parents."

ACTING AG BLANCHE REVEALS FATE OF TRUMP'S 'ANTI-WEAPONIZATION FUND' UNDER PRESSURE FROM HOUSE LAWMAKERS

"The effect of Merrick Garland and the DOJ and the FBI under the Biden administration issuing a threat tag, that was founded on the basis of using the Patriot Act against parents in this country that were showing up at school board meetings. It sent a chill through the country," Descovich said.

She continued to say that parents "need to not forget where we were in 2021 as we go into these midterm elections."

item.title: Alan Alda reveals unexpected weapon in his battle against Parkinson's disease
item.description: Alan Alda, now 90, reveals how humor and acceptance help him cope with Parkinson's disease, calling the condition "just a hobby" he lives with.
item.content:encoded:
Alan Alda is sharing his surprising method of coping with Parkinson’s.

The actor, 90, best known for portraying Captain Benjamin Franklin "Hawkeye" Pierce in the CBS wartime sitcom "M*A*S*H," was diagnosed with the degenerative motor disease in 2015 and publicly shared the news in 2018. 

The diagnosis came after the actor learned that his own behavior of acting out dreams could be an early Parkinson's symptom.

DAD JOKES MAY BE GOOD FOR YOUR BRAIN IN ONE SURPRISING WAY, EXPERTS SAY

"I had a symptom, which at the time was not that well-known: Acting out your dreams," he said in an Oct. 4 interview with CBS News. "I had a dream that somebody was attacking me. And I picked up a sack of potatoes and threw it at 'em. What I was really doing was throwing a pillow at Arlene, my wife."

Alda identified humor as his way of coping with the frustrations and limitations of the disease.

While he acknowledged the frustrations of the physical effects and limitations of Parkinson’s, he said "the best way to deal with anything that's a little bit of a problem is to find out what's funny about it and laugh at it."

In one example, he shared that when he has trouble controlling the computer mouse while composing an email, he personifies his condition as "Dr. Parkinson," moving his hand all over the screen and deleting things.

"I don't let Parkinson's define me," Alda said, joking that he sees the disease as "just a hobby."

PARKINSON’S PATIENT’S YEARS-LONG TREMOR VANISHES WITHIN MINUTES OF NEW ULTRASOUND TREATMENT

Rather than wishing he didn’t have the condition, the actor said he aims to accept his current reality.

"I really think reality is my friend," he said. "I don't want to wish it away. I can't wish it away. I can't hope for a better future. I gotta accept what is."

Although Alda acknowledged that everyday tasks, such as buttoning his shirt, have become difficult, he said he treats each one like a "puzzle" to solve.

"I do hate it, but the only thing that's helpful is: What haven't I tried? And pretty soon, you get the feeling, 'If I keep looking for new ways to try this, I'll get a solution.' It's a puzzle. Will I be able eventually to put my socks on? The last time I put my socks on was a tremendous moment to celebrate!"

SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISING BRAIN BENEFIT OF LAUGHTER: 'IT'S A MENTAL WORKOUT'

Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, agreed that humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.

"Humor involves cognitive reframing, this idea of looking at a circumstance through different angles — not necessarily changing the reality that one is in, but shifting the meaning and the emotional weight of the situation," Lane, who has not treated Alda, told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

When something feels frightening or distressing, such as a medical diagnosis, creating some "psychological distance" can make a "big, big change" in perspective, he added.

Connection is another important component of humor, Lane noted.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Humor is often shared. It brings us together," he said. "We are meant to share our lives with others. The importance of having a sense of belonging and humor can be a glue in that way, bringing us closer with others so that one does not go on the journey alone."

Lane shared that he has witnessed the power of humor and connection in his own practice as he cares for people living with Parkinson's disease.

"One of the wonderful things that I've seen in those settings is that, just like Mr. Alda, people crack a joke, [it] brings them a smile."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The neuropsychiatrist also noted that Alda’s acceptance of his condition is "enormously empowering."

"It's the idea of saying to oneself, what are the choices that I can make in the moment?" Lane told Fox News Digital. "Rarely do we ever have control over our entire day and certainly not our entire life, but we often do have control over what we choose in the moment."

"Our sense of agency is an important part of our emotional well-being."

item.title: Democrats debate Kamala Harris 2028 run as surrogate says party wants to 'move on' from 2024 loss
item.description: Kamala Harris allies questioned whether her respect within the Democratic Party translates to real support for a 2028 presidential election bid.
item.content:encoded:
Allies of former Vice President Kamala Harris, as well as Democratic surrogates, are questioning whether the former Democratic nominee would be the top choice within the party, weighing her name recognition and respect among Democrats against the notion that voters want to move on.

"People just want to move on," Fletcher Smith, a former state legislator in South Carolina and Biden 2020 surrogate, told The Washington Post. "We’ve got a number of younger generation of people who are capable of leading — we’ve got governors, we’ve got congresspeople, we have senators. I think what she needs to do is sit out 2028 and let some other people have a shot at saving our democracy."

Many Democratic allies noted Harris is well respected within the party, but questioned whether respect translated into support.

DEMOCRATS SHY AWAY FROM QUESTIONS ON WHETHER HARRIS SHOULD RUN FOR PRESIDENT IN 2028

"She’s extraordinarily popular in the party and people are very fond of her and want her to be treated with a lot of respect and deference — given all the due of someone in her position," Jamal Simmons, a former communications director for Harris, told the Post. "Many people see it as a service what she did in 2024, where she really stepped up for the party, stepped up for Joe Biden, stepped up for the country. There’s a lot of respect for her. But it’s yet to be seen how much of that becomes support for another presidential run."

Podcast host and former South Carolina state senator Bakari Sellers told the Post that though she is" very talented," she has yet to define what a potential 2028 run would look like to key constituencies.

"One of the first statements she put out was about AI, when it’s clear she needs to boost her support among Black men," Sellers told the Post. "California has a cost-of-living issue, and she’s not talking about cost of living at all."

The Post reported that Sellers said he hasn't spoken to Harris in over a year. He suggested that was concerning for a candidate who would need a victory in South Carolina, according to the report.

HARRIS STOPS IN KEY PRESIDENTIAL PRIMARY STATE AFTER LEAVING DOOR WIDE OPEN TO 2028 RUN

During Sellers' podcast on Monday, he listed Harris as No. 2 in his top five candidates for 2028. He said Harris was talented and intelligent, but questioned whether her team would "let her be great."

"Let Kamala be Kamala, and you would have the next president of the United States without a doubt in my mind," he said. The podcast host ranked Maryland Gov. Wes Moore in the No. 1 spot, calling him the "biggest impediment" to Harris being the nominee.

WATCH: DEM SENATORS DODGE BACKING KAMALA HARRIS IN POTENTIAL 2028 RUN: ‘VERY MESSY’

Democratic strategist Kaivan Shroff, who was part of Hillary Clinton's 2016 campaign, told Fox News Digital that Harris hasn't done anything differently since 2024.

"Harris has not done anything truly new or different since 2024. Her greatest post-VP visibility came from her book tour. Running again without a new chapter or story to tell is like reapplying to the same college after getting rejected, taking a gap year, and coming back with basically the same application. You can rewrite the essay, but if you did nothing new, admissions is still looking at the same file," Shroff said.

Shroff suggested somebody new might have the advantage over her because they would be introducing themselves to voters for the first time on a national stage.

"She does not get to reintroduce herself. That is the burden of being so well known. She has a real base and a lot of goodwill in the party, but she also lost, and that makes some voters and, importantly, donors nervous. Even if she starts high in the polls, the question is where the growth comes from if there is not much new to add," he said. "Someone like a Pritzker at least gets the advantage of telling his story to a lot of voters for the first time."

Shroff added, "What Harris is doing well right now is using her position as a party leader rather than acting like a candidate in waiting. A great example is her showing up for Abdul El-Sayed despite his criticism of her and the bad blood with some on the far left in Michigan. She acknowledged the disagreements, still made the case for him, and used her stature to help unite the party in a critical moment — particularly with outreach to Black voters. That is an example of influence she has right now, regardless of what she does in 2028 and that will continue to matter whether she seeks the nomination or not."

California Gov. Gavin Newsom said during a recent interview that he would not run in 2028 if Harris planned to run.

DEM MEGADONOR UNLEASHES REALITY CHECK ON HARRIS FOR 2028 WHILE EYEING SOCIALIST FIREBRAND

Harris has not been definitive on whether she plans to run, but has said she is thinking about it.

Others were more confident in Harris, including Ashley Etienne, another former communications director for the former VP. She told the Post that Harris would need to separate herself from the Democratic establishment, but said she would have major advantages in a national election.

CARVILLE DOESN'T 'FEEL SORRY' FOR URGING DEMOCRATS TO MOVE ON FROM THE KAMALA HARRIS ERA

"It’s almost like, why not her? She has proven, unlike anyone else in the race, that she’s got these advantages that will matter in a national election," she told the Post.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Virginia Democratic state senator L. Louise Lucas told the Post that Democrats rejecting Harris too fast could be interpreted as a negative political move as well, suggesting it could be seen as overlooking a qualified Black woman for the position.

"There’s no question that people would be upset because you see what happened last time," Lucas told the Post. "It could very well be that some folks would be so disillusioned that they would just say, ‘I give up on this process’ — especially people who’ve been fighting as many years as I have, who have come through the civil rights movement and just experienced so much, endured so much, and then to see this happen again would be quite painful."

Several members of Congress didn't rush to throw their support behind Harris when asked by Fox News Digital about her possibly running in 2028.

"Well, I've backed her before, but there'll be other contenders this time," Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., told Fox News Digital. "I've made no decisions about who I would support."

"I think we're going to have a very, very, very messy and very big primary," Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., said. "It's going to be every Tom, Dick and Harry. And that's probably where it should be."

"We're focused on 2026," said Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, D-Md. "We're going to win back the House and the Senate."

She continued, "I love Kamala Harris. I have a very personal friendship and relationship. She's amazing. I think anybody who wants to run should. She's obviously very well qualified. We need to focus on '26."

item.title: Trump, Waltz link France riots to mass immigration as thousands are arrested
item.description: Trump claims France's student protests are about "Islam wanting to take over" as Sébastien Lecornu reports the school system's heaviest toll in decades.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX: President Donald Trump warned Tuesday that France’s escalating riots were being driven by "out of control mass migration," as U.S. Ambassador to the U.N. Mike Waltz echoed those concerns and blamed unchecked immigration and broader European policy failures for helping fuel the unrest.

Asked by Fox News Digital about Trump’s comments and the scenes emerging from France, Waltz condemned the violence while also linking the unrest to European immigration and economic policies.

"I think we would always condemn lawlessness, condemn the violence that we're seeing in Paris," Waltz told Fox News Digital. "But I think we also have to recognize that when you have open borders, when you [have] this pro-migration, unchecked immigration kind of policy, coupled with policies over the years that deny people basic energy, that overspend on all kinds of other government programs, that you see a level of frustration boiling to the surface."

FRANCE EXPLODES AGAIN AS STUDENTS RIOT OVER EDUCATION

Trump weighed in as the unrest intensified, arguing that what was unfolding went beyond the students’ complaints about France’s education system. "What’s happening in France is nothing less than out of control mass migration. This isn’t about schools, this is about Islam wanting to take over a once great Country!" Trump wrote on Truth Social Tuesday.

"Unfortunately, I think you're seeing the results of some of that, and President Trump has brought that to light," Waltz added.

The comments came as France faced its biggest day of school unrest since the protests began in September. On Tuesday, police fired tear gas in Paris and other major cities, protesters lit fires and hurled projectiles, and France’s Interior Ministry said 6,100 people had been arrested, the overwhelming majority of them minors, according to Reuters. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu described the clashes as producing the school system’s "heaviest toll in decades".

FRANCE’S VIOLENT STUDENT PROTESTS RAISE WARNING FOR AMERICA: ‘A CAUTIONARY TALE’

France’s Interior Ministry said 6,100 people have been arrested so far, the overwhelming majority of them minors. Lecornu told lawmakers Tuesday that at least 215 teenagers and 85 school staff members have been injured, while his office said more than 700 police officers have also been hurt, according to Reuters.

The latest demonstrations brought clashes in Paris, Lyon, Strasbourg and Rennes, where police fired tear gas as protesters lit fires and hurled projectiles. More than half of France’s roughly 3,700 high schools were blockaded or expected to close Tuesday, according to the High School Students Union. The ⁠Paris police said the clashes there had come about when some 300 people attempted to face off against security forces, adding that the protest was generally unfolding well elsewhere.

Theo Wold, a former assistant attorney general and former White House deputy assistant for domestic policy under Trump, also argued that immigration was contributing to the unrest.

FRANCE ROCKED BY STUDENT RIOTS AS HUNDREDS ARRESTED, VIOLENCE SPREADS NATIONWIDE

"The French are notorious for strikes, labor stoppages and street demonstrations. It’s a core part of the Fifth Republic’s civic culture," Wold told Fox News Digital. "What’s new is the violence, lawlessness and rioting. This is a consequence of mass immigration."

While Trump, Waltz and Wold linked the violence to immigration, Reuters and AP have reported that the protest movement began over school conditions, including teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating buildings and education funding. Students have cited overcrowded classrooms, teacher shortages and deteriorating school buildings — including water leaks and rat infestations — among their grievances.

The unrest has increasingly become part of a broader political fight ahead of France’s presidential election in April and May 2027. Reuters reported last week that French authorities and political opponents have accused lawmakers and mayors from the hard-left France Unbowed party, or LFI, of stoking the demonstrations. LFI has denied the accusations.

Fox News Digital's Greg Norman-Diamond and Reuters contributed to this story.

item.title: Former All-Star pitcher 'Sudden' Sam McDowell dead at 84
item.description: Former All-Star pitcher Sam McDowell battled alcohol abuse that ended his career at 32, but his transformation into a sports psychology therapist redefined his legacy.
item.content:encoded:
Six-time All-Star pitcher Sam McDowell died Monday at 84.

The cause of death is unknown. KDKA first reported McDowell’s death.

McDowell pitched in the big leagues for 15 seasons, spending 11 of them with the then-Cleveland Indians, parts of two seasons with the San Francisco Giants, parts of two with the New York Yankees and his final season with the Pittsburgh Pirates.
