McDowell, nicknamed "Sudden Sam," won the American League ERA title in 1965 with a dazzling 2.18 ERA and made the first of his six All-Star Games that season. In his career, McDowell had a 141-134 record with a 3.17 ERA in 425 games.

The Pittsburgh native is in the Guardians Hall of Fame. McDowell made his MLB debut at 18 but was out of baseball by 32 in 1975 because of alcohol abuse.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

"I was the biggest, most hopeless and most violent drunk in baseball," McDowell told the New York Post in 2001. He recalled jumping off of hotel balconies into swimming pools.

In that same interview, McDowell said he had lost his family and career to alcohol. He went to rehab in 1978 and turned things around. He went back to college and became a licensed therapist in sports psychology and addictions.

McDowell then returned to baseball, working for the Toronto Blue Jays and Texas Rangers. From 1987-2016, he served as an addiction and recovery consultant for the Baseball Assistance Team.

"I truly believe with all my heart, the greatest thing that ever happened to me was that I was an alcoholic and found out about it," McDowell said. "Had I never known and had not been thrown out of baseball, I would not have the great life I have now. I would not have the education. I would not have learned how to live and love. Every day is a kick."

item.title: The hotel TV privacy mistake that can follow you home
item.description: Hotel TV privacy risks go beyond forgotten passwords when you sign into Netflix or other streaming apps on shared devices you don't control.
item.content:encoded:
You've just arrived at your hotel after a long day of travel. The room looks good, the bed looks comfortable and there's a big TV on the wall with Netflix and your other favorite streaming apps ready to go. So, you grab the remote, sign in and settle in for the evening. Seems harmless, right?

Here's the part that's easy to forget. That TV was used by plenty of guests before you, and more will use it after you leave. If you sign into a streaming service and forget to log out, your account could still be accessible after you've checked out and headed home. Before you reach for the remote, here's what to know about hotel TV privacy and the safer ways to stream while you're traveling.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways AI can help you get better health care.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class Get Better Healthcare with AI has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways AI can help you prepare for appointments, remember important details, understand complicated medical information, research prescription questions and organize your next steps. No technical experience is needed.

Plus, recordings of all our past classes are available, including How to Stop Spam, Phone Security and Financial Protection, each with a free downloadable checklist.

Watch the free replays and get your checklists at CyberGuyLive.com

TRAVEL MISTAKE PUTS PHONE, LAPTOP AND STREAMING ACCOUNTS AT RISK

A hotel TV isn't your TV at home. It's a shared device that you don't control. When you sign into a streaming service, the app may create and store a session on that television so you don't have to log in every time you turn it on. That doesn't necessarily mean your password is sitting on the TV in plain text. But if the session stays active after you leave, the next person in the room may be able to open the app and use your account.

Depending on the streaming service, that could let someone watch shows using your subscription, switch between profiles or see parts of your viewing activity. Netflix itself warns that a TV from a recent hotel stay can remain connected to your account. Its Manage Access and Devices feature lets you review recently active devices and sign them out remotely.

There is another wrinkle here. Some newer hotel entertainment systems are designed specifically for guests and offer secure casting from your phone instead of requiring you to enter streaming credentials on the TV. Some of these systems automatically disconnect your device when you check out. That's a much better setup when it's available. Still, you can't assume every hotel TV works that way.

Smart TVs can also collect information about what's being watched. Some television platforms use technology called Automatic Content Recognition (ACR) to identify content displayed on the screen and collect viewing information. The exact tracking depends on the TV, its software and its privacy settings.

That doesn't mean every hotel television is tracking you personally or connecting your Netflix identity to everything you watch. Hotel TVs can use specialized commercial software and configurations that work differently from the smart TV sitting in your living room. But it's another reason I wouldn't treat a hotel television like one of my personal devices.

FLORIDA SUES NETFLIX, ALLEGES STREAMER TRACKED CHILDREN AFTER PROMISING FAMILIES PRIVACY

My preference is simple: keep your streaming accounts on devices you control. Your phone, tablet or laptop already has your streaming apps and account information. If you want to watch on the larger hotel screen, first check whether the hotel offers a casting option that lets you connect from your own device without entering your password on the TV.

If it doesn't, an HDMI cable can be another option. Connect your laptop to the TV and switch the television to the correct HDMI input. Depending on your phone or tablet, you may also need a compatible USB-C or other video adapter. HDMI carries audio, video and certain control signals between devices, but connecting your laptop this way generally does not give the hotel TV access to the passwords, documents or other personal files stored on your computer. One caution: some hotel TVs have locked inputs or hotel equipment connected to the HDMI ports. If you disconnect anything to use the port, put it back exactly as you found it before you check out.

Hotel Wi-Fi deserves some attention too, although there's an important distinction here. Most major websites and streaming services use HTTPS encryption, which means your password and other information aren't simply sitting out in the open for another hotel guest to read.

Still, you're connecting through a network you don't control. A VPN adds another layer of privacy by encrypting the connection between your device and the VPN server. If you use a VPN when traveling, turn it on before connecting to sensitive accounts or doing other private browsing. A VPN service can help reduce what the hotel network or Wi-Fi operator can see about your internet traffic. Just remember that a VPN doesn't make you invisible online. The streaming service you're using still knows you're connected to it.

For the best VPN software, see my expert review of the best VPNs for browsing the web privately on your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

BEFORE YOU CONNECT ANOTHER SMART TV, TABLET OR PHONE, LOCK IT DOWN

If you're reading this from your hotel room and you're signed into Netflix or another streaming service on the TV, there's no reason to panic. Before you leave, open the streaming app and choose Sign Out. Don't assume that closing the app or turning off the TV signs you out. If you've already checked out and can't remember whether you logged out, do this:

Look in your streaming service's account or security settings for recently active devices. Netflix has a Manage Access and Devices section that lets you remotely sign out individual devices.

If you see a device you don't recognize or one that appears to be the hotel TV, remove it.

Check profiles and viewing activity for anything you don't recognize.

Use a strong, unique password for that streaming account. A password manager can help you create and store a long, random password so you don't have to reuse one from another account. If you're changing a Netflix password, keep the Sign out all devices option selected so existing sessions are removed.

Some streaming accounts use verification codes or other additional checks for certain sign-ins and account changes. Turn on any additional account protection your service provides.

I've stayed in enough hotels to know how tempting it is to drop your bag, turn on the TV and sign straight into Netflix. But I don't like putting my account credentials into a device I don't own, especially when I have other options sitting right in my bag. If the hotel offers secure casting from your phone, that's the first thing I'd look for. Otherwise, I'll use my own laptop or mobile device and connect to the television when possible. I also like using a VPN on hotel Wi-Fi for an added layer of privacy on a network I don't control. And if you do sign directly into that hotel TV, add one thing to your checkout routine: log out before you walk out the door. It takes a few seconds and could save you from discovering days later that somebody else is still enjoying your streaming account.

item.title: Hazmat crew removes 'glass vials,' vacuum from home linked to missing women in potential serial killer probe
item.description: Police seized glass vials, a vacuum and workout equipment from the Philadelphia house of horrors once owned by pornographer Raymond Horsch.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE PHOTOS: PHILADELPHIA — Police have returned again to a home in Philadelphia's Olney neighborhood, where they collected "glass vials," a vacuum cleaner, workout equipment and other items, photographs show.

This is after city police have said they recovered more than a million pieces of digital evidence from the home, described as a "house of horrors" in some reports.

It used to belong to a pornographer named Raymond "RC" Horsch, who died last year at 82.

PHILLY SERIAL KILLER PROBE COULD EXPOSE LARGER NETWORK BEHIND APPARENT 'SNUFF' FILMS, EXPERT SAYS

One evidence bag was photographed with a partially legible label. It listed "glass vials," a "board" as well as references to a bin and drawers.

Investigators were also seen taking out a rowing machine and a vacuum cleaner among boxes and bags of packaged evidence Monday.

"The investigation remains active and ongoing," a Philadelphia police spokesperson told Fox News Digital Tuesday. "Additional information will be released as it becomes available and is appropriate for public release."

Horsch specialized in sadistic themes — some of which may ultimately prove to be nonfiction after investigators say evidence in the home has been linked to seven separate cases involving missing women.

GILGO BEACH SERIAL KILLER REX HEUERMANN KEPT 'DEXTER'-STYLE KILL ROOM BUT WASN'T AS SMART AS HE THOUGHT: DA

Philadelphia police have repeatedly revisited the building following the June arrest of his 44-year-old son, Eugene Horsch, on drug, firearms and forgery charges.

While searching the home after his arrest, police allegedly found "snuff" videos believed to show multiple missing women, a drum of chemicals hooked up to the water system and five urns that contained what police said might be human ashes.

PHILADELPHIA HOME LINKED TO 7 MISSING WOMEN, LATE RESIDENT'S POTENTIAL 'SERIAL KILLER' MEMOIR INVESTIGATED

FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X

Four of the seven missing women believed to be connected to the home have been identified in those images, according to authorities.

Only some of them have been publicly identified. Philadelphia police identified Maribel Fresses, 26, who vanished in 2018, and Gabrielle Aramando, 27, earlier in the investigation.

During Eugene Horsch's arrest, the woman with him had an ID for Blair Tonzelli, 38, who was last seen in Philadelphia in February 2023, police told Fox News Digital in September.

Two other women were identified in local reports. Both are listed as missing persons in the National Missing and Unidentified Person System, or NamUs.

One is Horsch's ex-wife, Amy McHale, 54, who was 44 when she was last seen on June 13, 2016, the Philadelphia Inquirer reported in June.

The other is Nicole "Nikki" Fusaro, 34, according to CBS' Philadelphia affiliate, citing local police sources.

She was 27 when she vanished near the intersection of Kensington and Allegheny Avenue in July 2019.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM THE FOX TRUE CRIME HUB

Investigators said they have also identified dozens of other people from the images.

Excavation crews have previously been seen searching outside and under the home, including the sewers.

GOT A TIP?

The younger Horsch has not been charged in connection with any of the missing women. But at the time of his unrelated arrest in a BMW at the city's Independence Mall, authorities allege that the woman with him was carrying one of their IDs.

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

Dr. Kris Mohandie, a board-certified forensic psychologist, has warned that the elder Horsch may have been part of a wider network centered on the production and distribution of "snuff films."

GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL

"The fact that the father was involved in the pornographic industry indicates that there may have been, in addition to the sadistic motives that we usually see in serial murders, that there may have been profit in distribution of so-called snuff films," he told Fox News Digital previously.

The older Horsch was a convicted producer of methamphetamines and an author of sexually explicit and violent books. In one, 2014's "Empathy," there is a chapter about dissolving a murdered woman's body with boiling chemicals.
